name: macos-swiftui
summary: macOS SwiftUI structure with explicit app, windows, features, shared UI, services, models, and test boundaries.
dependency_direction: App -> Windows/Commands -> Features -> SharedUI / DesignSystem -> Services -> Models.

folders.responsibility: App entry, app scene composition, dependency assembly.
folders.allowed: App lifecycle, settings scene, root dependency setup.

folders.responsibility: Window scene, command, toolbar, and placement behavior.
folders.allowed: Window controllers, scene definitions, command groups, toolbar composition.
Feature views, view models, feature state.
folders.avoid: Global services and unrelated shared utilities.

folders.allowed: Controls, modifiers, layout primitives, status views.

folders.responsibility: Project UI tokens, platform UI rules, and component policy.
folders.allowed: Color tokens, typography scales, spacing constants, system component wrappers.
folders.avoid: UI-system or third-party wrappers that conflict with existing conventions or require unapproved dependencies.

folders.responsibility: System, persistence, network, file, and app service boundaries.
folders.allowed: File access wrappers, persistence adapters, network clients, platform services.

folders.responsibility: Shared data structures and domain types.

folders.allowed: Unit tests, integration tests, UI-adjacent test fixtures.

rules: Preserve the existing deployment target, build settings, window behavior, design system, and component conventions before choosing new APIs.
Use native SwiftUI/system components, semantic colors and type, and SF Symbols when they fit the product, accessibility needs, and confirmed deployment target.
Follow the project's established desktop density, spacing, typography, and token conventions instead of imposing an iOS-derived or generic palette.
Support keyboard shortcuts and menu commands where the product workflow or accessibility contract calls for them.
Use SwiftUI or a narrow AppKit bridge according to capability, compatibility, and existing project conventions; document a bridge when its boundary is non-obvious.

Use Liquid Glass or another current Apple design language only when the confirmed target supports it, the product wants it, and current official documentation validates the approach; do not raise deployment targets or restyle an existing product by default.
Verify current Apple developer documentation before implementing newly introduced platform UI APIs.
Do not install third-party UI libraries without explicit authorization and a demonstrated need.
When visual direction is incomplete, preserve existing design signals or propose a coherent option and label assumptions instead of waiting for a fixed second phase.
Separate window behavior from feature business logic.
validation: Use the macOS build/run/debug workflow when available.
Verify window, command, toolbar, and settings behavior after UI changes.
